rows.evidence: Q1: Case study section (Figures 2-4, Table 3) - authors compute their own dekadal anomaly percentiles and drought onset/duration/severity statistics for the 2014 Senegal drought from CHIRPS, H SAF, ESA CCI, SWI, NDVI and VODCA datasets.
rows.notes: The paper is labelled a Review; only the Senegal case study is original analysis. That analysis shows microwave SM and VOD anomalies tracking the 2014 drought; it does not report any own result on crop development, crop yield monitoring or any crop production outcome (yield deficits are cited from ARC/EM-DAT/GIEWS reports, not analysed). The review's statements on yield (Carrao 2016, Padhee 2017, Modanesi 2020) are cited work and do not count. Soil moisture drought detection is at most a precondition of the claimed yield/crop-development benefit.

rows.evidence: Q1: Case study section (Figures 2-4, Table 3) - authors' own anomaly-percentile analysis of satellite rainfall, soil moisture and vegetation datasets for the 2014 Senegal drought.
rows.notes: No own result on irrigation scheduling optimization or water conservation. Irrigation is mentioned only incidentally (satellite SM implicitly includes irrigation water, citing Massari 2021; a region near Guiers Lake/Senegal river was 'most likely' less affected due to irrigation - an unverified interpretation). The case study demonstrates microwave soil moisture assessment for drought monitoring, which is at most a precondition of the claimed irrigation-scheduling benefit.

notes: Document is a review article (Frontiers in Water, type 'Review') with an embedded Senegal case study that is the only original analysis; it concerns drought monitoring with microwave SM/VOD anomalies, not irrigation scheduling or crop yield. Q1 answered yes on the strength of the case study; if the case study is not accepted as a primary contribution, Q1 would be no with the same downstream profile.
